headings.text: 2 Minimum static friction on an incline

html:
The big picture

The lecture finishes the friction problems of 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction and opens three new topics, two of them as "intermissions". (1) The block-and-pulley system with sliding friction is solved by substitution: the shared acceleration is a = g\,(m_2 - m_1\mu_D)/(m_1 + m_2). (2) A box on an incline stays put only if \mu_S \ge \tan\alpha. (3) The weight F_G = mg is a special case of universal gravitation F_G = G m_1 m_2/r^2; when gravity acts as the centripetal force of a circular orbit, it gives the orbital period of the Moon or a GPS satellite. (4) Work W = \int_L \vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s is force times displacement along it; lifting a mass by H stores the work as potential energy E_\text{pot} = mgH, and conservation of energy says the total never changes. (5) A forklift fails by tipping about its front wheel, which force balance can't describe. The tool is torque, force × lever arm, and rotational equilibrium \sum T_P = 0 gives the load limit m x = M L.

1 Coupled bodies with sliding friction

Lecture: photos 1–2 (summary p. 1) · Giancoli §5-1

This finishes the system of 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction: block m_1 on a table, joined by a rope over a pulley to the hanging block m_2. Board, left edge: the knowns m_1, m_2, \mu_D. Small sketch next to the result: block 1 on the table, arrow a to the right; block 2 hanging, arrow a down.

EQUATIONS FROM LAST WEEK:

\begin{aligned} &\text{I} && \textstyle\sum F_y = 0 = F_R - F_{G2} + m_2\cdot a \\ &\text{II} && \textstyle\sum F_x = 0 = F_R - F_{F1} - m_1\cdot a \\ &\text{III} && \textstyle\sum F_y = 0 = F_{N1} - F_{G1} \\ &\text{IV} && F_{F1} = \mu_D\cdot F_{N1} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • m_1 — mass of the block on the table (kg); m_2 — mass of the hanging block (kg)
  • F_{G1} = m_1 g, F_{G2} = m_2 g — their weights (N), down
  • F_R — rope force (N), the same along the whole rope (massless rope, frictionless pulley)
  • F_{N1} — normal force of the table on block 1 (N), up
  • F_{F1} — sliding friction on block 1 (N), to the left, against the motion
  • \mu_D — dynamic (sliding) friction coefficient between block 1 and the table (dimensionless)
  • a — size of the shared acceleration (m/s²): block 1 to the right, block 2 down
  • m_1 a, m_2 a — d'Alembert inertial forces (N), drawn against the acceleration; x to the right, y up

Each body has its own free-body diagram, written in d'Alembert's form "\sum F - m a = 0" with the inertial force counted against the acceleration. I is block 2 vertically: rope up, weight down, inertial force up (block 2 accelerates down). II is block 1 horizontally: rope right, friction left, inertial force left. III is block 1 vertically: no vertical motion, so the normal force balances the weight. IV is the sliding-friction law. One a for both, because the rope doesn't stretch. Four unknowns (F_{N1}, F_{F1}, F_R, a), four equations: substitute until only a is left.

Substitution (board order): from III, F_{N1} = F_{G1} = m_1\cdot g; ↳ in IV, F_{F1} = \mu_D\cdot m_1\cdot g; IV in II, 0 = F_R - \mu_D\cdot m_1\cdot g - m_1\cdot a \Rightarrow F_R:

F_R = m_1\cdot(a + \mu_D\cdot g) \;\to\; \text{I}

Symbols as above. (Add \mu_D m_1 g + m_1 a to both sides of II, factor out m_1.) "\to I" means this F_R now goes into I, the only equation not yet used:

\begin{aligned} 0 &= m_1 a + m_1\mu_D g - m_2 g + m_2 a && \text{(I with } F_R \text{ inserted; the two } a\text{-terms circled)} \\ m_2\cdot g - m_1\,\mu_D\cdot g &= a\cdot(m_1 + m_2) && \text{(}g\text{-terms to the left, factor out } a) \\ a &= g\cdot\frac{m_2 - m_1\,\mu_D}{m_1 + m_2} && \text{(factor out } g\text{, divide by } m_1 + m_2) \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. Boxed on the board: a = g\,(m_2 - m_1\mu_D)/(m_1 + m_2) and a \ge 0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

"a \ge 0": a was defined as the size of the acceleration in the direction "block 2 goes down". The formula holds only while the system really slides that way, which needs m_2 \ge \mu_D m_1. If it gives a < 0, the sliding model doesn't apply; a system at rest stays at rest while m_2 g \le \mu_S m_1 g. Inserting a into F_R gives F_R = \dfrac{m_1 m_2\,(1 + \mu_D)\,g}{m_1 + m_2}. Sanity checks: \mu_D = 0 gives a = \frac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\,g; m_1 \to 0 gives a \to g; units m/s² ✓.

Worked example — the system with numbers

m_1 = 3\,\mathrm{kg}, m_2 = 2\,\mathrm{kg}, \mu_D = 0.25.

  1. Acceleration: a = 9.81 \cdot (2 - 0.75)/5 \approx 2.45\,\mathrm{m/s^2}.
  2. Rope force: F_R = 3 \cdot (2.45 + 2.45) \approx 14.7\,\mathrm N.
  3. Check with I: 14.7 - 19.62 + 2 \cdot 2.45 \approx 0 ✓. A second set of numbers is in 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction.
Unclear (summary p. 1 vs board photo 2): a > 0 or a \ge 0

The board's boxed condition reads "a \ge 0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}". The AI summary prints "a > 0". This note follows the board. The difference matters only for the borderline case m_2 = \mu_D m_1, a system already sliding at constant speed.

2 Minimum static friction on an incline

Lecture: photos 3–5 (summary p. 2) · Giancoli §5-1

QUESTION: If we know \alpha, what must be the minimum value for \mu_S such that box "m" does not slide?

Board sketch: a slope falling to the right at angle \alpha to the horizontal, box m on it, \mu_S marked at the contact.

STEP 1 → FREE BODY DIAGRAM (FBD). Board FBD (coloured chalk): weight m\cdot g = F_G straight down, split into F_{Gx} (along the slope, downhill) and F_{Gy} (into the slope). The friction F_F points up the slope and the normal force F_N is perpendicular to it. Axes: x along the slope pointing downhill, y perpendicular to the slope, away from it. STATIC PROBLEM, so \Rightarrow a = 0\ \mathrm{m/s^2}.

With x along the slope, friction and F_{Gx} lie on one axis and F_N and F_{Gy} on the other; only the weight has to be split.

Board: the force triangle of the weight. On the left, the first try with "\alpha?" at both candidate corners. In the middle, the answer: \alpha sits between F_G and F_{Gy}, with the right angle between F_{Gy} and F_{Gx}. Below, a reminder: a force F at angle \alpha to the horizontal, and the x–y axes.

F_{Gx} = F_G\cdot\sin\alpha, \qquad F_{Gy} = F_G\cdot\cos\alpha

The same split in the book's picture: the weight m\vec g (straight down) splits into mg\sin\theta along the slope and mg\cos\theta into it; the normal force balances only the second. The angle between m\vec g and the slope's normal equals the slope angle. The book writes \theta for the lecture's \alpha. (Giancoli Fig. 4-26b)

Symbols
  • F_G = m g — weight of the box (N), straight down
  • F_{Gx} — component of the weight along the slope, downhill (N)
  • F_{Gy} — component of the weight into the slope (N)
  • \alpha — slope angle from the horizontal

Why \alpha sits at the top of the triangle (the "\alpha?"): F_G is perpendicular to the horizontal and F_{Gy} perpendicular to the slope; two angles whose sides are pairwise perpendicular are equal. In the right triangle F_G is the hypotenuse, F_{Gy} lies next to \alpha (\cos), F_{Gx} opposite (\sin). Check: on flat ground (\alpha = 0) nothing pulls sideways and the full weight presses down ✓.

Common mistake — swapping sin and cos on the slope

Tempting: "the component along the slope is F_G\cos\alpha", because \alpha "belongs to the slope". Check \alpha = 0: a flat floor would then pull the box sideways with its full weight, which is absurd. Do the \alpha \to 0 check every time.

STEP 2: EQUATIONS

\begin{aligned} &\text{I} && \textstyle\sum F_x = 0 = F_{Gx} - F_F = m\cdot g\cdot\sin\alpha - F_F && \Rightarrow\ F_F = m g\sin\alpha \\ &\text{II} && \textstyle\sum F_y = 0 = F_N - F_{Gy} = -m\cdot g\cdot\cos\alpha + F_N && \Rightarrow\ F_N = m g\cos\alpha \\ &\text{III} && F_F = \mu_S\cdot F_N && \Rightarrow\ m g\,\sin\alpha = \mu_S\cdot m g\,\cos\alpha \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • F_F — static friction on the box (N), up the slope
  • F_N — normal force of the slope on the box (N), perpendicular to the slope, away from it
  • \mu_S — static friction coefficient (dimensionless); m — mass of the box (kg)

(I and II "\Rightarrow III" on the board; in the last line both factors mg are crossed out.) So \sin\alpha = \mu_S\cos\alpha, and the MINIMUM VALUE for \mu_S:

\boxed{\,\mu_S = \frac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha} = \tan\alpha\,}

Symbols as above. Why "minimum": static friction can be anything up to \mu_S F_N, so the box stays while mg\sin\alpha \le \mu_S\,mg\cos\alpha, i.e. \mu_S \ge \tan\alpha. Setting III with "=" picks the borderline. Mass and g cancel: a heavy and a light box of the same material start sliding at the same angle, which is how \mu_S is measured.

Unclear (board photo 5): a stray "P" under equation III

Below "\mu_S" in line III the board has a short line with a "P" under it. It isn't used anywhere and the AI summary drops it. Its meaning is unclear (perhaps a leftover from an erased line).

Worked example — how rough must a ramp be?

A loading ramp rises at \alpha = 25^\circ. Will a crate stay put with \mu_S = 0.4? With \mu_S = 0.5?

  1. Minimum needed: \mu_{S,\min} = \tan 25^\circ \approx 0.466.
  2. Compare: 0.4 < 0.466, so the crate slides; 0.5 > 0.466, so it stays.
  3. Reverse question: with \mu_S \approx 0.9 (rubber on asphalt), the steepest angle that still holds is \arctan 0.9 \approx 42^\circ.
Problem-solving steps — a body on an incline
  1. Draw the FBD: weight down, normal force perpendicular to the slope, friction along the slope against the (tendency of) motion.
  2. Tilt the axes: x along the slope, y perpendicular.
  3. Split only the weight: along mg\sin\alpha, into the slope mg\cos\alpha; check with \alpha \to 0.
  4. \sum F_y = 0 gives F_N = mg\cos\alpha; \sum F_x = m a (or 0) with the friction law.
  5. "Just about to slip" → F_F = \mu_S F_N; sliding → F_F = \mu_D F_N.

3 Gravitation

Lecture: photos 8–10 (summary pp. 3–4), "Intermission: gravitation" · Giancoli §6-1, §6-3, §6-4, §6-5

F_G = m\cdot g \quad\text{which comes from } F = m\cdot a

\Downarrow ACTUALLY COMES FROM

\boxed{\,F_G = G\cdot\frac{m_1\cdot m_2}{r^2}\,} \qquad \text{units: } \mathrm N = \frac{\mathrm{N\,m^2}}{\mathrm{kg^2}}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{kg^2}}{\mathrm{m^2}}

UNIVERSAL GRAVITATIONAL CONSTANT:

G = 6.67430\cdot 10^{-11}\ \frac{\mathrm{N\,m^2}}{\mathrm{kg^2}}
Symbols
  • F_G — gravitational force between two bodies (N); attractive, along the line joining them; each feels the same size of force (reaction principle)
  • m_1, m_2 — masses of the two bodies (kg)
  • r — distance between their centers (m), not between their surfaces
  • G — the universal gravitational constant, the same everywhere
  • m, g — in F_G = mg: mass of a body on Earth (kg) and the gravitational acceleration at the surface (m/s²)

Universal gravitation: every two masses attract each other, with a force proportional to both masses and falling off with the square of the distance (an inverse-square law): double the distance and the force drops to a quarter. "Universal": the same law, with the same G, for an apple and for the Moon. For spheres, r is measured between centres, as if all the mass sat there. G is tiny: two 1 kg masses 1 m apart attract with 6.7\cdot10^{-11}\,\mathrm N. The unit line checks that the right side is a force; that is how the unit of G is chosen.

The direction of the force: m_2 pulls m_1 straight towards itself along the line joining them (\vec F_{12}, opposite to the unit vector \hat r_{21} pointing from m_2 to m_1). By axiom 3, m_1 pulls m_2 back equally hard. (Giancoli Fig. 6-6)

What "actually comes from" means. F_G = mg is universal gravitation for a body at the Earth's surface (m_1 = m, m_2 = M_E, r = r_E):

m\,g = G\,\frac{m\,M_E}{r_E^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g = \frac{G\,M_E}{r_E^2}
Symbols
  • M_E — mass of the Earth (kg); r_E — radius of the Earth (m); g — surface gravitational acceleration (m/s²)

EARTH (board): M_\text{EARTH} \approx 5.97\cdot10^{24}\ \mathrm{kg}, r_E \approx 6379\ \mathrm{km}; on the sketch g \approx 9.83\ \mathrm{m/s^2} at the pole, \approx 9.81 at 45^\circ, \approx 9.78 at the equator. Inserting: g = \frac{6.674\cdot10^{-11} \cdot 5.97\cdot10^{24}}{(6.379\cdot10^{6})^2} \approx 9.79\ \mathrm{N/kg} = 9.79\ \mathrm{m/s^2} ✓ (\mathrm{N/kg} = \mathrm{m/s^2}). g varies because the Earth is slightly flattened (poles closer to the centre) and because at the equator part of gravity is used as the centripetal force of the Earth's daily rotation, about \omega^2 r_E \approx 0.034\ \mathrm{m/s^2}. 9.81 is the mid-latitude value used in calculations.

Board: the Earth with radius r_E and the three g values. A dashed distance "DIST" runs to the MOON (labelled "(SATELLITE)"), which moves on (dotted arrow). The force F_G points from the Moon to the Earth. Below: "SOMEHOW", F_G circled = F_{CP}, and the centripetal formulas.

Orbits. F_G \overset{\text{SOMEHOW}}{=} F_{CP} = m_M\cdot a_{CP} ("CENTRIPETAL FORCE"):

a_{CP} = r\cdot\omega^2, \qquad \omega = \frac{v}{r}, \qquad a_{CP} = r\cdot\frac{v^2}{r^2} = \frac{v^2}{r}
\omega = 2\pi f, \qquad f = \frac1T, \qquad \omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} \;\to\; \approx 28.2\ \text{days}
Symbols
  • F_{CP} — centripetal force (N): the net force toward the centre that keeps a body on a circle
  • m_M — mass of the Moon (kg); a_{CP} — centripetal acceleration (m/s²)
  • r — orbit radius, from the Earth's centre to the Moon (m); v — orbital speed (m/s)
  • \omega — angular velocity (rad/s); f — frequency (Hz); T — orbital period (s)

On a circle a body needs a net force toward the centre of size m\,a_{CP} (7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion). The centripetal force is not an extra force but the job some real force has to do; for the Moon, gravity does it and nothing else acts. So F_G = F_{CP}, which is the "SOMEHOW". The calculation the board skips:

\begin{aligned} G\,\frac{m_M\,M_E}{r^2} &= m_M\,r\,\omega^2 && \text{(}F_G = F_{CP}\text{, with } a_{CP} = r\omega^2) \\ \omega^2 &= \frac{G\,M_E}{r^3} && \text{(divide by } m_M r\text{: the Moon's mass cancels)} \\ T &= 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{G\,M_E}} && \text{(insert } \omega = 2\pi/T\text{, solve, positive root)} \end{aligned}

Symbols as above. For the Moon (r \approx 3.844\cdot10^{8}\,\mathrm m): T \approx 2.37\cdot10^{6}\,\mathrm s \approx 27.5 days, within 1 % of the measured 27.3 days. Units: \sqrt{\mathrm m^3/(\mathrm{N\,m^2\,kg^{-2}}\cdot\mathrm{kg})} = \mathrm s ✓. The orbiting body's mass cancels: a satellite at the Moon's distance would circle in the same time. Larger orbits are slower, T^2 \propto r^3 (Kepler's third law).

Unclear (board photo 9): "\approx 28.2 days"

The board's result for the Moon, "\approx 28.2 days", doesn't follow from the lecture's data. With G, M_E = 5.97\cdot10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg} and r = 384\,400\,\mathrm{km}, the formula gives about 27.5 days. The measured orbital (sidereal) period is 27.3 days, the cycle of Moon phases 29.5 days. 28.2 days would need r \approx 391\,000\ \mathrm{km}. Most likely a rounded distance was used; the board doesn't show the inputs.

Worked example — period of the ISS

The ISS flies about 420\ \mathrm{km} above the ground. How long is one orbit?

  1. Orbit radius from the Earth's centre: r = r_E + h = 6379 + 420 = 6799\ \mathrm{km} = 6.799\cdot10^{6}\ \mathrm m.
  2. Period: T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(6.799\cdot10^{6})^3}{6.674\cdot10^{-11} \cdot 5.97\cdot10^{24}}}\ \mathrm s \approx 5580\ \mathrm s \approx 93 min.
  3. Speed: v = 2\pi r/T \approx 7.66\ \mathrm{km/s}.
  4. Check: about 15–16 orbits a day, as reported for the ISS ✓.
Common mistake — altitude instead of distance, and "no gravity in orbit"
  1. In G m_1 m_2/r^2, r is measured from the Earth's centre. Inserting the altitude (420 km) instead of r_E + h gives a gravity 260 times too strong.
  2. Astronauts float not because gravity is missing: at the ISS altitude g = GM_E/r^2 \approx 8.6\ \mathrm{m/s^2}, 88 % of the surface value. They float because they and the station fall together; gravity is entirely used as the centripetal force, so nothing presses them against the floor.

EXERCISES (board): Calculate the orbital period of a "GPS" satellite (GNSS) using F_G = G\,\dfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2} and centripetal force. GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) is the general term; GPS (USA) and Galileo (EU) are examples. It is the Moon calculation with a different r: look up the satellites' altitude and add r_E. Check against the design goal: GPS satellites circle the Earth twice a day.

Problem-solving steps — circular orbits
  1. Orbit radius from the centre of the central body: r = r_E + h.
  2. Set gravity equal to the centripetal force: G\frac{mM}{r^2} = m\frac{v^2}{r} = m r\omega^2; the orbiting mass cancels.
  3. Solve for what is asked: v = \sqrt{GM/r}, T = 2\pi\sqrt{r^3/(GM)}, or r from a given T.
  4. Convert days/hours to s and km to m before inserting; check the units come out in s or m/s.

4 Work and energy

Lecture: photos 11–13 (summary p. 5), "Work & energies" · Giancoli §7-1, §7-3, §8-2, §8-5

The board introduces two quantities: WORK & ENERGIES, W … Work, E … Energies / Energy. Work is the energy a force transfers to a body by pushing it along. The book builds it up in the same steps as below: a constant force first, then a force that changes along the path, then the energy that work stores, then its conservation. 11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy continues each step.

Work done by a constant force. Board sketch: a box m is pushed by a force F to the right over the distance s; friction F_F acts on it to the left. If the force is constant and points along the displacement, the work is force times distance:

When the force is at an angle \theta to the motion, only its part along the displacement does work: W = F\cos\theta \cdot d. The board's case is \theta = 0, where \cos\theta = 1. The book writes d for the lecture's s. (Giancoli Fig. 7-1)

W = F\cdot s, \qquad W = F_F\cdot s, \qquad [F] = \mathrm N, \quad [s] = \mathrm m, \quad [W] = \mathrm{Nm},\ \mathrm J,\ \mathrm{Ws}
Symbols
  • W — work (J)
  • F — constant pushing force, parallel to the displacement (N)
  • F_F — friction force on the box (N), opposite to the motion
  • s — distance moved (m)
  • J (joule) = \mathrm{N\,m}; Ws (watt-second) = \mathrm J, since 1\,\mathrm W = 1\,\mathrm{J/s}

W = F_F\cdot s: to slide the box at constant speed you push exactly as hard as friction holds (a = 0), so F_F s is the work you do against friction. The friction force itself points against the motion (\cos 180^\circ = -1), so the work done by friction on the box is -F_F s; that energy becomes heat in the box and floor. The units: [W] = \mathrm N\cdot\mathrm m, named joule; the electricity unit Ws is the same (1 Physical Quantities and the SI System). If the force is at an angle \theta to the motion, only its component along the motion counts: W = F s\cos\theta, the scalar product \vec F\cdot\vec s (2 Vectors and Vector Products › 6 Scalar product ("dot product")); worked out in 11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 5 Work done by a constant force.

Unclear (summary p. 5 vs board photo 13): the friction line and the unit line

The board writes "W = F\cdot s", "W = F_F\cdot s" and "[W] = \mathrm{Nm}, \mathrm J, \mathrm{Ws}". The AI summary prints "W_F = Fs and W_\text{friction} = -F_F s" and "[\mathrm J] = \mathrm{N\cdot m} = \mathrm{W\cdot s}". The minus sign and subscripts are not on the board; they are the summary's interpretation (correct for the work done by friction). Which sign convention the exam expects is unclear.

Common mistake — "holding or carrying something is work"

Carrying a heavy bag across a flat room is hard, so it's tempting to say you do work on it. Your force points up, the bag moves horizontally: \cos 90^\circ = 0, so W = 0 on the bag. Your muscles use energy internally, but none is transferred to the bag. Work needs a force component along the displacement.

Carrying a bag across the room: the hand's force \vec F_P points up, the displacement \vec d sideways. They are perpendicular, so W = F_P\,d\cos 90^\circ = 0. (Giancoli Fig. 7-2)

The general case: a varying force along a curved path. When the force changes along the way or the path bends, F\cdot s no longer works. The board's general definition:

W = \int_L \vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s \qquad L \to \text{LINE INTEGRAL}, \quad \mathrm d\vec s \to \text{DISTANCE / DISPLACEMENT}
Symbols
  • W — work done by the force \vec F on the body along the path (J)
  • \vec F — the force (N), possibly changing along the path
  • \mathrm d\vec s — a tiny piece of the displacement along the path (m)
  • L — the path; \int_L adds up the contributions of all its pieces
  • \cdot — scalar (dot) product

Cut the path into tiny straight steps \mathrm d\vec s. On each step the force is practically constant, and its contribution is \vec F\cdot\mathrm d\vec s = F\,\mathrm ds\,\cos\theta, with \theta the angle between force and step: only the part of the force along the motion counts. \int_L adds up all contributions. (The board writes the vectors without arrows; the dot product is needed for the sign.) Work is positive when the force has a component along the motion, negative when against it, and zero when the force is perpendicular to the motion (the normal force on a sliding box). For a constant force along a straight path every step contributes the same, and the integral collapses to F\cdot s above. The spring, where the force grows with the stretch, is the standard varying-force example (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 6 Work done by a varying force: the spring).

Worked example — work against friction vs work against gravity

A 20\,\mathrm{kg} crate. Compare (a) pushing it 5\,\mathrm m across a floor at constant speed with \mu_D = 0.3 and (b) lifting it 1.5\,\mathrm m.

  1. (a) Force needed: constant speed, so F = F_F = \mu_D m g = 0.3 \cdot 20 \cdot 9.81 \approx 58.9\ \mathrm N.
  2. (a) Work: W = F\cdot s = 58.9 \cdot 5 \approx 294\ \mathrm J, all of it becoming heat.
  3. (b) Work: W = m g H = 20 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 1.5 \approx 294\ \mathrm J, all of it stored as E_\text{pot} (next paragraph).
  4. Point: the same work, but only the lifted crate can give the energy back as motion.
Problem-solving steps — work by a constant force
  1. Identify which force's work is asked (yours, friction's, gravity's).
  2. Find its size F and the angle \theta between force and displacement.
  3. W = F s\cos\theta: positive along the motion, negative against it, zero across it.
  4. Lifting by H: W = mgH = E_\text{pot}; work against sliding friction at constant speed: \mu_D F_N s, ending as heat.
  5. Check units: J = N·m.

POTENTIAL ENERGY. Board sketch: a box m is lifted from the ground (a stick figure stands there) to a height H; weight m\cdot g. Lift the box slowly (no acceleration): your force just balances the weight, F = F_G = mg, pointing up along the motion, over the distance H:

W = F_G\cdot H, \qquad \boxed{\,E_\text{pot} = m g H\,}
Symbols
  • W — work needed to lift the box (J); F_G = mg — its weight (N)
  • H — height lifted, measured from a chosen zero level, here the ground (m)
  • E_\text{pot} — potential energy of the box at height H (J)

Potential energy is energy stored by position. The work put in is not lost: let go, and gravity does the work mgH on the box as it falls back. Only differences in height matter, so the zero level can be chosen freely. Lifting 12\,\mathrm{kg} onto a 2\,\mathrm m shelf costs 12 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 2 \approx 235\ \mathrm J. This works because gravity is a conservative force: the work it does depends only on the start and end height, not on the path; the general definition, \Delta E_\text{pot} = -W_g, is in 11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 8 Potential energy.

ENERGY IS PRESERVED — NO ENERGY IS LOST:

\boxed{\,\Delta E_\text{over time} = 0\,}
Symbols
  • E — total energy of a closed system: all forms together (potential, motion, heat, …) (J)
  • \Delta E — its change between any two moments (J)

Conservation of energy: in a closed system (no energy flowing in or out) energy changes form, but its total stays the same. "No energy is lost" refers to the total: in the friction example mechanical energy seems to disappear but reappears as heat. This lets you skip forces and time: a box falling from H turns mgH into energy of motion, and with the kinetic energy \tfrac12 m v^2 this gives the impact speed v = \sqrt{2gH}, the Torricelli equation of 5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 9 Conservation of energy).

5 Torque and equilibrium: the forklift

Lecture: photos 6–7 (summary p. 3), "Intermission: forklift" · Giancoli §10-4, §12-1, §12-2

Board, "INTERMISSION — FORKLIFT". A forklift with driver and body mass M; its centre of mass is at horizontal distance L from the front wheel. The load m on the fork sits at distance x in front of the mast. The front wheel is marked "TILTING POINT". Below: a beam on a pivot \Delta with a force F on the left and F_2 on the right; F_2 is drawn again further out (dashed). To the right: a column "m: 100, 200, 300, …, 1000" and "COM →".

A forklift doesn't fail because a force balance breaks; it fails by tipping forward about its front wheel, the tilting point. Describing that needs the turning effect of a force, and the conditions under which a body doesn't turn.

Torque. The turning effect of a force about a pivot is its torque. The same push on a door turns it easily at the handle and hardly at all next to the hinge, and not at all if you push straight toward the hinge. What counts is the force times its distance from the pivot, measured perpendicular to the force. The lower board sketch shows it: on a beam over the pivot \Delta, moving F_2 further out (dashed) makes the same force turn the beam harder. For a force perpendicular to the line to the pivot:

A door seen from above, hinge on the left: the same force turns it more easily far from the hinge (F_A at lever arm R_A) than close to it (F_B at R_B). (Giancoli Fig. 10-11)

A force at an angle: only the part perpendicular to the arm, F_\perp = F\sin\theta, turns the door; the part along the arm, F_\parallel, pushes into the hinge and does nothing. So T = R\,F_\perp. The board's d is this perpendicular lever arm. (Giancoli Fig. 10-14)

T = F\cdot d
Symbols
  • T — torque about the pivot (N·m); the board's letter, often written \tau (the AI summary and Giancoli do) or M in German texts; sign by the turning sense
  • F — size of the force (N)
  • d — lever arm: perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action (m)

A force through the pivot (d = 0) has no turning effect. Sign: the board fixes "CCW +": counter-clockwise torques count positive, clockwise ones negative, the same convention as for angles in 7 Rotational Kinematics and Circular Motion › 1 Angular position. This is the same "force × lever arm" balance as the lever rule in 3 Center of Mass; in vector form torque is the cross product \vec T = \vec r \times \vec F (2 Vectors and Vector Products › 7 Vector product ("cross product")).

Common mistake — torque and work have the same unit, so they're the same thing

Both come out in N·m. In work, force and displacement point along each other (dot product); the result is energy, written in joules. In torque, force and lever arm are perpendicular (cross product); the result is a turning effect, always written N·m, never J.

The conditions for equilibrium. A body at rest stays at rest only if it neither starts to move nor starts to turn: the forces must cancel and the torques about any point must cancel,

\textstyle\sum \vec F = \vec 0, \qquad \sum T = 0
Symbols
  • \sum\vec F — sum of all forces on the body (N); \sum T — sum of all torques about a chosen point (N·m), with signs
Why does a body at rest need both \sum F = 0 and \sum T = 0?

\sum \vec F = \vec 0 only says that the centre of mass doesn't accelerate. Two equal and opposite forces that don't act along the same line, like your hands on a steering wheel, sum to zero yet turn the body. Rotation is controlled separately, by the torques. So a rigid body is in equilibrium only when both the forces and the torques about any point cancel. The pivot can be chosen freely; choosing it where unknown forces act (here P) removes them from the equation, which is why the board takes torques about the tilting point.

Applying it to the forklift. The forklift's own weight Mg acts behind the front wheel (at distance L) and holds the rear down; the load's weight mg acts in front of it (at distance x) and tries to lift the rear. The column 100 … 1000 is most likely the list of loads m (kg) to lift, each with its own maximum distance x, the idea behind a forklift's load chart. "COM →" points back to 3 Center of Mass: Mg acts at the forklift's centre of mass, which defines L.

Board, simplified model: a horizontal beam on the pivot P. M\cdot g (down) acts at distance L to the left of P, m\cdot g (down) at distance x to the right. Rotation sense "CCW +".

\sum F_y = 0 \;\to WON'T WORK. Vertically there are four forces: two weights and the ground's support at the front and rear wheels, both unknown. More importantly, force balance can't say whether the forklift rotates: tipping is a rotation, so the torque condition is needed. Just before the forklift tips, the rear wheel is about to lift off (its support force is 0), and the forklift doesn't rotate yet, so the torques about P cancel. Mg left of P turns counter-clockwise (+MgL); mg right of P turns clockwise (-mgx); the support at P has lever arm 0:

\textstyle\sum T_P = 0 = -m\cdot g\cdot x + M\cdot g\cdot L, \qquad m g x = M g L, \qquad \boxed{\,m\, x = M\cdot L\,}
Symbols
  • T_P — torque about the pivot P, the tilting point (N·m)
  • M — mass of the forklift with driver (kg), acting at its centre of mass
  • L — horizontal distance from P to the forklift's centre of mass (m): the lever arm of Mg
  • m — mass of the load (kg); x — horizontal distance from P to the load (m): the lever arm of mg
  • CCW + — counter-clockwise torques positive, clockwise negative

(Add mgx, divide by g.) The forklift is safe while m x \le M L: the load's "mass × distance" may not exceed the forklift's own. Double the distance and the allowed load halves. The board: "100\ \mathrm{kg} at x = 1\ \mathrm m \to 50\ \mathrm{kg} at x = 1\ \mathrm m".

Unclear (board photo 7): "100 kg at x = 1 m → 50 kg at x = 1 m"

As written, both lines have x = 1\ \mathrm m. With m x = M L, the product stays fixed: 100\ \mathrm{kg} \cdot 1\ \mathrm m = 100\ \mathrm{kg\,m}, so 50 kg belongs to x = 2\ \mathrm m. The second "x = 1\,\mathrm m" is most likely a slip for x = 2\ \mathrm m; alternatively it could mean "the same position, but a forklift half as heavy". Ask in the tutorial.

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §10-4)

If the force is not perpendicular to the line from the pivot, only its perpendicular part turns: T = r\,F\sin\theta = r\,F_\perp, with r the distance from the pivot to the point of action and \theta the angle between \vec r and \vec F. The lever arm is d = r\sin\theta, so this is the same as F\cdot d.

Worked example — a load chart for a small forklift

A forklift with driver has M = 2500\,\mathrm{kg}; its centre of mass is L = 0.6\,\mathrm m behind the front wheel. What is the largest load at x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5\,\mathrm m?

  1. Tipping limit: m_\text{max} = \dfrac{M L}{x}, with M L = 1500\,\mathrm{kg\,m}.
  2. Insert: x = 0.5\,\mathrm m: 3000\,\mathrm{kg}; x = 1.0\,\mathrm m: 1500\,\mathrm{kg}; x = 1.5\,\mathrm m: 1000\,\mathrm{kg}.
  3. Check with torques at x = 1.0\,\mathrm m: load 1500 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 1.0 = 14\,715\,\mathrm{N\,m} clockwise, forklift 2500 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 0.6 = 14\,715\,\mathrm{N\,m} counter-clockwise ✓.
  4. Meaning: real forklifts carry this as a load chart, with a safety margin below the limit.
Common mistake — "a heavy enough forklift can lift anything"

The tipping condition is m x \le M L: what counts is mass times lever arm. A light load far out on the forks can tip a forklift that easily carries a much heavier load held close to the mast.

Problem-solving steps — tipping and rotational equilibrium
  1. Choose the body and find the point it would turn about (tilting point, hinge, pivot).
  2. Draw all forces with their points of action; the support at the pivot drops out of the torque equation.
  3. For each force, find the lever arm (perpendicular distance to the pivot) and the turning sense (CCW +).
  4. At the tipping limit, set \sum T_P = 0 and solve; safe side: the restoring torque is larger. If more unknowns remain, add \sum F_x = 0, \sum F_y = 0.
  5. Check units (N·m) and that a larger lever arm needs a smaller force.
Connection

Torque about a joint is what every robot-arm motor must deliver; the forklift balance m x = M L is the calculation that tells you how heavy a payload an arm can hold at full reach. Work and energy come back as power (\mathrm{W} = \mathrm{J/s}) when sizing motors and batteries. Orbital mechanics is the basis of the GNSS positioning used by outdoor mobile robots.
